# Results — Study 925 (Front-End Trend) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The rule: read the **3-month
(63 trading-day) change in `^IRX`**, the 13-week Treasury bill yield. Front-end yield
**falling** → hold **TLT** (20y+ Treasuries); **rising or flat** → hold **BIL** (1-3 month
bills). Binary, no shorting, **one** execution lag (signal formed through the close of day
`t`, acted at `t+1`), 2 bps one-way × NAV charged on each switch. Every arm is measured
**excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's own total return), so nothing gets credit for merely
parking in bills while bills paid 5%. ETF legs are **total-return** closes (`yfinance`,
`auto_adjust=True`); `^IRX` is a **price-only yield level** used as a signal input and
never as a return. Common SHY∩IEF∩TLT∩BIL∩^IRX window 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30 (BIL's 2007
inception gates the tradable cash leg). As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current month is
dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SHY, IEF, TLT, BIL (total return) + ^IRX (yield, price-only) | 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30 | 4,800 | Fingerprint `c05691fe8719` |

The rule holds duration **47.8%** of the days and switches **321** times (~17/yr).

## The race — excess-of-cash

The random control holds TLT on *random* days at the **same** 47.8% in-market frequency —
but it pays for ~2,400 coin flips, so read it beside the flip-free **matched blend**
control below, which carries the same average exposure with no switching at all.
Drawdowns are the *absolute* (lived) max drawdown, not the excess one.

| Arm | Excess Sharpe | Excess CAGR | Vol | Max drawdown | HAC *t* (mean) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Switch (front-end trend)** | **+0.154** | +1.09% | 10.98% | −28.2% | +0.73 |
| **Static IEF (7-10y)** | **+0.293** | +1.82% | 6.99% | −23.9% | +1.37 |
| Static TLT (20y+) | +0.184 | +1.66% | 15.24% | −48.4% | +0.89 |
| Random control (one seed) | −0.316 | −3.74% | 10.37% | −47.2% | −1.39 |

- **Excess-Sharpe advantage (switch − static IEF): −0.139**, HAC *t* on the daily return
  difference = **−0.20**. Against static TLT the difference *t* is **−0.52**. Neither is
  anywhere near |*t*| = 2, and the point estimate has the **wrong sign**.
- The switch arm is *more* volatile than the static intermediate holding it is meant to
  improve on (11.0% vs 7.0%) and drawdowns deeper (−28.2% vs −23.9%): it is not a risk
  reducer either.

## Bootstrap CIs (2,000 draws, 21-day circular blocks)

| Quantity | Point | 95% CI | share < 0 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Switch excess Sharpe | +0.154 | [−0.283, +0.554] | 24.3% |
| Static IEF excess Sharpe | +0.293 | [−0.136, +0.704] | 9.3% |
| Static TLT excess Sharpe | +0.184 | [−0.236, +0.588] | 20.2% |
| **Sharpe difference (switch − IEF)** | **−0.139** | **[−0.498, +0.221]** | 76.4% |

The paired difference CI straddles zero with three-quarters of the mass on the losing
side. On this tape you cannot tell the switch rule apart from just owning IEF — except
that its central estimate is worse.

## The random control is a turnover trap (the honest correction)

A single random-control seed makes the rule look like a genuine timer: **+0.469** excess
Sharpe, *t* = +2.01. That is one draw of 4,800 coin flips. Swept over **30 seeds**:

| Cost | Advantage vs random (mean) | sd | range | *t* (mean) | share with *t* ≥ 2 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 bps (net) | **+0.268** | 0.177 | −0.125 … +0.629 | +1.20 | 20% |
| **0 bps (gross)** | **+0.060** | 0.175 | −0.328 … +0.414 | **+0.29** | **0%** |

The "genuine timing" **evaporates gross**. A frequency-matched coin flips about
`2p(1−p)N` ≈ 2,400 times against the rule's 321, so at any positive cost the control is
handicapped by turnover it never chose. What looked like skill was the rule's *lower
turnover*, not its *better days*.

## The control the random one should have been: a matched constant-weight blend

The clean way to ask "is the *timing* worth anything?" is to hold the rule's **average**
exposure with **no flips at all**: a constant **47.8% TLT / 52.2% BIL** book, rebalanced
daily (drift trades only — 91%/yr of turnover, charged at the same cost the rule pays).
Same duration on average, no regime switching, no seed to draw.

| Cost | Switch exSharpe | Matched blend exSharpe | Advantage | Return-diff *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 bps (headline) | +0.154 | **+0.182** | **−0.028** | +0.23 |
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.185 | **+0.184** | **+0.001** | +0.43 |

Gross, the rule and the flip-free blend of identical average exposure are **the same
number to two decimals** (+0.185 vs +0.184, a gap of one part in a thousand); net, the
blend is ahead. So the timing decisions — 321 of them
over nineteen years — are collectively worth **zero**, and the *only* control the rule ever
beat was the one paying seven times its trading costs. (The return-difference *t* is mildly
positive while the Sharpe advantage is negative: the switch earns a hair more per day but
carries more volatility for it. Neither is close to significant.)

## Day-level conditional test (gross, no portfolio construction)

The cleanest read of whether the signal carries information at all — the excess-of-cash
daily return of TLT, split by what the rule said the day before:

| Days | n | Mean excess TLT return | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| "Own duration" (front end falling) | 2,263 | **+1.69 bp/d** | +0.87 |
| "Sit in bills" (front end rising) | 2,473 | +0.59 bp/d | +0.36 |
| **Spread** | | **+1.09 bp/d** | **HAC *t* = +0.43** (Welch *t* = +0.39) |

The spread's *t* is the **HAC** one: the buckets are picked by a signal that persists for
months, so daily returns inside a bucket are anything but independent draws and Welch's
iid *t* is reported for reference only. Right sign, no significance either way. Nineteen
years of daily data cannot separate the two buckets.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2016-01-01)

| Era | n | IEF exSharpe | Switch exSharpe | Advantage (*t*) | In duration | IEF DD → switch DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007–2015 | 2,100 | +0.73 | +0.28 | **−0.452** (*t* = −0.71) | 58% | −10.4% → −27.1% |
| 2016–2026 | 2,635 | −0.11 | +0.03 | **+0.138** (*t* = +0.44) | 39% | −23.9% → −28.2% |

The sign **flips** between halves and neither half is significant. The recent-era "win" is
mostly the 2022 dodge (see the calendar table); the early era is a straight loss.

## Robustness — lookback sweep (is 63 days special?)

| Lookback | Switch exSharpe | Advantage (*t*) | In duration | Switches |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 21d | +0.377 | **+0.056** (*t* = +0.99) | 45% | 615 |
| 42d | +0.129 | **−0.178** (*t* = −0.41) | 47% | 424 |
| **63d (headline)** | +0.154 | **−0.139** (*t* = −0.20) | 48% | 321 |
| 126d | +0.144 | **−0.122** (*t* = −0.11) | 52% | 205 |
| 252d | +0.353 | **+0.083** (*t* = +1.25) | 53% | 116 |

The advantage changes **sign three times** across a perfectly reasonable grid of windows
and never clears the bar in either direction. There is no window at which the idea works;
there are only windows where the noise happens to point up.

## Cost sensitivity (no short leg → no borrow; switch friction only)

| One-way cost | Switch exSharpe | Advantage (*t*) | Max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.185 | −0.108 (*t* = −0.01) | −27.9% |
| 2 bps (headline) | +0.154 | −0.139 (*t* = −0.20) | −28.2% |
| 5 bps | +0.107 | −0.186 (*t* = −0.49) | −28.7% |
| 10 bps | +0.029 | −0.264 (*t* = −0.96) | −29.8% |
| 25 bps | −0.203 | −0.496 (*t* = −2.35) | −50.3% |

At ~17 switches a year friction is not decisive, but it is never a rescue: the advantage is
already negative gross and only walks further into the red.

Absolute total returns. **All twenty calendar years** are printed (a hand-picked subset
would prove whatever the picker wanted; this table is the whole record).

| 2011 | +26.4% | +15.6% | +34.0% | **+10.7** | 73% |
| 2012 | +4.5% | +3.7% | +2.4% | +0.8 | 20% |
| 2013 | −14.8% | −6.1% | −13.4% | −8.7 | 59% |
| 2014 | +24.9% | +9.1% | +27.3% | **+15.9** | 73% |
| 2015 | −11.3% | +1.5% | −1.8% | **−12.8** | 38% |
| 2016 | +2.7% | +1.0% | +1.2% | +1.7 | 24% |
| 2017 | −1.4% | +2.6% | +9.2% | −3.9 | 2% |
| 2018 | +1.7% | +1.0% | −1.6% | +0.7 | 0% |
| 2019 | +6.9% | +8.0% | +14.1% | −1.2 | 67% |
| 2020 | +6.1% | +10.0% | +18.2% | −3.9 | 83% |
| 2021 | −15.2% | −3.3% | −4.6% | **−11.9** | 56% |
| **2022** | **+1.4%** | −15.2% | −31.2% | **+16.5** | **0%** |
| **2023** | **+21.0%** | +3.6% | +2.8% | **+17.3** | **15%** |
| 2024 | −9.4% | −0.6% | −8.1% | −8.8 | 71% |
| 2025 | +8.8% | +8.0% | +4.2% | +0.8 | 72% |
| 2026 (partial) | +1.8% | −0.1% | +1.0% | +1.9 | 47% |

**Beats IEF in 11 of 20 years; mean gap −0.10 pp/yr, median +0.76 pp/yr.** The coin-toss
hit rate with a slightly negative mean is exactly what a no-information rule looks like.

Two of those years are *timing* years, and they are the ones everyone remembers. **2022**:
the front end rose all year, the rule sat in bills for **0 of 251 sessions** in duration,
and beat IEF by 16.5 points. **2023**: it held duration for exactly **37 sessions,
2023-11-06 → 2023-12-29**, during which **TLT gained +14.7%**; the rule's own compounded
return over that stretch was **+16.2%** (it was in bills for the one down session inside
the window), and bills paid ~4.9% for the other eleven months.

The other big gaps are **not** timing. In 2011 (+10.7) and 2014 (+15.9) the rule simply
happened to be long a TLT that returned +34% and +27% — it *lagged* its own instrument
both times and beat IEF only because 20-year duration beats 8-year duration in a bull
market. The symmetric price is 2009 (−14.9), 2015 (−12.8) and 2021 (−11.9), where it held
that same duration into the sell-off. Strip the beta and what is left is 2022 and 2023 —
two episodes in nineteen years, which is not a sample.

## Cross-check — the same bet read off SHY instead of ^IRX

Replace the yield change with **SHY's 12-minus-1-month total-return momentum** (a rising
short-bond price *is* a falling front-end yield):

- switch **+0.331** vs static IEF **+0.270** → advantage **+0.061** (*t* = **+1.43**),
  in duration **85%** of days, only **68** switches.
- gross vs the random control over 30 seeds: **+0.172** (mean *t* = **+1.36**).
- **vs its own matched blend** (constant 85.2% TLT / 14.8% bills): **+0.153** net
  (*t* = **+1.92**), **+0.158** gross (*t* = **+1.97**).

This is the strongest number in the study and it must be reported as such: measured against
a fixed-weight book of its *own* average exposure, the SHY-momentum variant keeps about
0.15 of Sharpe, and it keeps it gross. It still does not clear |*t*| ≥ 2 — and it is not
stable:

| Slice | n | in duration | Advantage vs matched blend (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007–2015 | 1,911 | **99%** | **+0.005** (*t* = +0.51) |
| 2016–2026 | 2,635 | 75% | **+0.243** (*t* = +1.52) |
| Full sample **excluding 2022** | 4,296 | 90% | **+0.156** (*t* = +1.24) |

In the first half the rule was long duration on 99% of days — it made no decisions to be
right about, and its advantage is +0.005. Everything it has comes from the second half,
where the 2022 hiking cycle is the dominant event; drop 2022 and the *t* falls to +1.24.
So the honest reading is: a nearly-always-long-duration holding whose edge over IEF
(+0.061) is mostly TLT beta, plus one genuinely well-timed hiking cycle that a single
alternative specification, below the bar and concentrated in one era, cannot establish as
skill. It is the piece of this study most worth someone else's attention — not a badge.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

The knob is the AR(1) coefficient on the short rate's daily *increments*, with
unconditional rate volatility held fixed, so the worlds differ in predictability only.

- **Planted trending front end** (`signal_strength=1`): advantage **+1.78**
  (*t* = **+4.66**); across 10 seeds mean **+2.15**, fires (adv ≥ 0.4) in **10/10**.
- **Random-walk null** (`signal_strength=0`): advantage mean **−0.050** (sd 0.203),
  |adv| ≥ 0.4 in **0/10**.
- The **matched-blend control has power too**: on the planted world the switch beats its own
  constant-weight blend by **+1.545** (*t* = **+4.45**), and on the null by −0.034. A
  control that never separates anything would prove nothing about the real tape.

The detector recovers a real front-end trend easily and stays silent when there is none.
The real-tape blank is therefore a fact about the US front end since 2007, not a broken
harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — None.** The claim is that the front of the curve trends persistently enough
  to pick your duration. On the real tape the switch rule's excess-of-cash Sharpe
  advantage over a static intermediate holding is **−0.139** (HAC *t* = **−0.20**), the
  paired bootstrap difference CI is **[−0.498, +0.221]**, the sign **flips** across eras
  (−0.45 / +0.14) and **three times** across the lookback grid, and the day-level
  conditional spread is +1.09 bp/d at HAC *t* = +0.43. The one result that looked like
  skill — beating a frequency-matched random control — is a **turnover artefact**: over 30
  control seeds it is +0.268 net but only **+0.060 gross** (mean *t* +0.29, 0/30 clear
  *t* ≥ 2), because the coin flips 2,400 times and the rule 321. Against the flip-free
  control of identical average exposure — a constant 47.8% TLT / 52.2% bills book — the
  rule is **+0.001 gross and −0.028 net**: the timing is worth nothing at all. Nothing
  here clears |*t*| ≥ 2 in the direction of the claim.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is no edge to bank. The switch arm delivers a *lower*
  excess Sharpe, *higher* volatility (11.0% vs 7.0%) and a *deeper* drawdown (−28.2% vs
  −23.9%) than the static IEF it replaces, at ~17 round trips a year. It is negative gross
  and more negative at every cost level tested.
- **The strongest counter-evidence, stated plainly.** The SHY 12-1 momentum expression of
  the same bet beats a fixed-weight book of its own average exposure by **+0.153** net /
  **+0.158** gross (*t* = +1.92 / +1.97). That is the best number in the study, it is not a
  turnover artefact, and it is still below |*t*| ≥ 2 — and it is +0.005 in the first half of
  the sample, where the rule held duration on 99% of days. One alternative specification,
  era-concentrated, under the bar: interesting, not evidence.
- **What is real and worth keeping.** The rule genuinely sat out all of 2022 (0 of 251
  sessions in duration) and genuinely held duration through the 37 sessions of late 2023 in
  which TLT gained +14.7% — those are not artefacts, and they are why the idea keeps
  getting rediscovered. Its other large winning years (2011, 2014) are duration *beta*, not
  timing: it was long a TLT that returned +34% and +27% and lagged it both times. Strip the
  beta and the record is two loud episodes inside nineteen years, which is exactly the
  shape of a coin that landed heads twice in a row where everyone was watching.
